description: Achankovil Sastha Temple is in Achankovil, within Aryankavu panchayat in Kollam district, Kerala, close to the Achankovil river. It is dedicated to Sastha, called locally Achankovil Andavan or Achankovil Arasan, and is listed by Wikipedia among five major Sastha temples of Kerala, with Kulathupuzha, Aryankavu, Sabarimala and Kanthamala. The deity is portrayed as a householder with two consorts, Purna and Pushkala, one on each side, and the complex has subordinate shrines including Bhagavati, Ganesha, Kartikeya, Durga and Nagaraja, plus a serpent grove. Local tradition holds that the idol was consecrated by Parashurama. The temple is known for a traditional snakebite remedy of sandalwood paste and herbal medicine, and the deity is revered as a healer; Wikipedia notes the evidence is largely anecdotal, and prompt medical care remains essential after a bite. Festivals include the ten-day Mandala Puja in the Malayalam month of Dhanu, the Revathi Puja in Makaram and a chariot festival, the Therottam. According to Wikipedia, the Travancore Devaswom Board administers the temple and the architecture is Dravidian in style.

description: Airavatesvara Temple stands at Darasuram, a locality beside Kumbakonam in Thanjavur district, Tamil Nadu, and is dedicated to Shiva. According to Wikipedia it was built by the Chola king Rajaraja II in the mid-twelfth century, with completion placed around 1166 CE. By tradition, its name comes from Indra's white elephant Airavata, said to have regained its white colour after worshipping Shiva at this site. The sanctum houses a lingam of roughly 1.5 metres beneath a vimana about 24 to 25 metres high, depending on the source. The Rajagambhiram mandapa is shaped like a stone chariot with carved wheels and horses, and the pillars and friezes show Puranic episodes and the lives of the Nayanmar saints. A separate shrine honours the goddess. Smaller than the Thanjavur and Gangaikondacholapuram temples, it is valued for the detail of its carving. It belongs to the UNESCO-listed Great Living Chola Temples.

description: Jogulamba Temple at Alampur, Jogulamba Gadwal district, Telangana, stands on the Tungabhadra near its meeting with the Krishna. Wikipedia describes the goddess Jogulamba as a form of Shakti, shown seated on a corpse with a scorpion, frog and lizard on her head; the name is said to mean mother of yogis. Shaktism lists Alampur among the eighteen Maha Shakti Peethas, where Sati's upper teeth are held to have fallen. Wikipedia reports an origin around the 7th century CE and destruction by the Bahmani Sultans in 1390, with the icon sheltered in the nearby Bala Brahmeswara temple until the shrine was rebuilt at its original site in 2005. The setting is the Navabrahma temple complex, nine Shiva temples attributed to the Badami Chalukyas of the 7th-8th centuries. The Telangana tourism site mentions an Alampur site museum established in 1952. The temple was included in the Government of India's PRASAD pilgrimage scheme in 2019, according to Wikipedia.

description: Sri Veera Venkata Satyanarayana Swamy Temple crowns Ratnagiri Hill at Annavaram, in Kakinada district (formerly East Godavari), Andhra Pradesh, close to the Pampa River. The deity is Satyanarayana, a form of Vishnu, worshipped with Anantha Lakshmi and Shiva. The district tourism page describes the cylindrical main image as joining the Hindu Trinity in a single form. According to temple tradition recounted on Wikipedia, a Brahmin and a local ruler dreamed that Vishnu wished to be installed on the hill; the idol was found beneath a Krishna Kutaja tree and consecrated on 6 August 1891, and the shrine was rebuilt in stone in 1933-34. The two-storey temple is designed to resemble a chariot with four wheels. It is best known for the Satyanarayana Vratam, performed in a mandapam on the premises, with large gatherings during the month of Karthika. The district tourism page also lists a Kalyana Mahotsavam of the deity, which it places in May. The Andhra Pradesh Endowments Department administers it through the Devasthanam.

description: Arunachaleswarar Temple, also called Annamalaiyar Temple, stands at the foot of the Arunachala hill in Tiruvannamalai, Tamil Nadu. It is dedicated to Shiva, worshipped as Annamalaiyar in the form of a fire lingam, with Parvati as Unnamulai Ammai. It is counted among the Pancha Bhoota Sthalams, the five Shiva temples linked to the natural elements, and here the element is fire. According to Wikipedia, the present masonry dates to the Chola period, with major additions under the Vijayanagara rulers, and the eastern Rajagopuram, about 66 metres and eleven tiers tall, was completed under the Nayaks. Wikipedia describes the complex as covering roughly 10 hectares. The temple is praised in the Tevaram hymns. Its best-known festival is Karthigai Deepam, held in the Tamil month of Karthigai, which ends with a flame lit on the hill. Devotees also walk the roughly 14 km girivalam circuit around the hill, especially on full-moon days. According to Wikipedia, the Tamil Nadu HR&CE Department currently administers the temple.

description: Attukal Bhagavathy Temple stands at Attukal on the banks of the Killi river in Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala, roughly two kilometres south-east of the Sree Padmanabhaswamy Temple. The presiding deity is Attukal Amma, regarded as Bhagavathy, a form of Bhadrakali or Parvati, and is often identified with Kannaki, the heroine of the Tamil epic Silappadikaram. According to traditional accounts, the goddess appeared as a young girl to the head of the Mulluveettil family and later directed him in a dream to consecrate her at a spot marked by signs. Shiva and Ganesha are among the other deities worshipped. The temple is best known for the Attukal Pongala, a ten-day festival in the Malayalam month of Kumbham (February-March) in which women cook sweet rice offerings in clay pots in the open. According to Wikipedia, the Guinness Book of World Records recorded the gathering in 1997 and again in 2009; the Attukal Temple Trust expected 3.5 to 4 million women at the 2026 Pongala on 3 March.

description: Brihadisvara (Brihadeeswarar) Temple stands in Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu, on the south bank of the Cauvery, and is dedicated to Shiva, worshipped as a large linga in the sanctum. UNESCO records that the Chola king Rajaraja I (r. 985-1012 CE) began construction possibly in 1003-1004 CE and consecrated it in 1009-1010 CE. The granite main tower, or vimana, has thirteen tiers crowned by an octagonal sikhara; UNESCO gives its height as about 59.82 m, though other publications quote figures near 63 m. The complex includes a colonnaded enclosure with sub-shrines, an entrance gopura and a monolithic Nandi. UNESCO notes mural paintings and carvings of 81 of the 108 karanas on the walls. The temple was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 1987 and forms part of the Great Living Chola Temples. According to Wikipedia, the Archaeological Survey of India protects the monument, while the Thanjavur Palace Devasthanam, whose hereditary trustee is head of the Thanjavur Maratha family, manages the temple. The Brahan Natyanjali dance festival is held around Maha Shivaratri.

description: The Buddha Temple is a small Buddhist shrine in Buddhamangalam village, Kilvelur taluk, Nagapattinam district, Tamil Nadu. It is dedicated to the Buddha, shown in a seated image on a pedestal whose face is no longer clearly visible. Wikipedia describes it as one of the earlier Buddhist centres in Tamil Nadu but gives no date for the shrine or the image. The Way of Bodhi website reports that the statue was found in the surrounding fields and is now kept in a newly built vihara beside them, which local people said was funded by a group of Buddhists from Thailand. It explains the village name as meaning an auspicious place of the Buddha. Both sources describe the site as poorly maintained, and Way of Bodhi adds that window grills at the vihara had been stolen. The village is a farming community, so visitors should expect a modest rural site rather than a developed pilgrimage centre.

description: The Buddha Temple at Perunjeri (also spelled Perunchery) is a Buddhist shrine in Mayiladuthurai district, Tamil Nadu, said to lie about half a kilometre off the Sundrappanchavadi-Kilianur road on the Mayiladuthurai-Thiruvarur route. According to Wikipedia, its main image is a Buddha statue about 5 feet 3 inches tall (another account gives about 5 feet 7 inches), showing the tradition's usual iconographic features: tightly coiled hair, a flame-like crest above the head, elongated ears and an upper garment. The pedestal carries a Tamil inscription that is reported to be faint and hard to read. Wikipedia notes the statue was originally found about a furlong from the present shrine, and gives no date for either the statue or the temple; one independent account assigns the image to roughly the 8th to 10th century CE. The shrine is still in use, with local people lighting lamps before the image. It belongs to the wider group of Buddha images that survive in the Kaveri delta region, several of which a 2014 Dinamalar report described as poorly maintained. No detailed history, trust or visiting arrangements are documented in the sources consulted.

description: Chakkulathukavu Sree Bhagavathy Temple is a Devi temple at Neerattupuram in Thalavady panchayat, Alappuzha district, Kerala, near Thiruvalla and on the banks of the Pampa river. The presiding deity, Chakkulathamma, is regarded as a form of Durga. The temple's own account also mentions a Vana Durga idol, subsidiary shrines to Shiva, Sastha, Vishnu and others, and an adjoining Hanuman shrine. Its founding legend, as told by the temple, speaks of a hunter who came upon a sand-covered shell that the sage Narada opened to reveal a Vana Durga image, and the temple states that it is almost 3,000 years old, a claim not independently dated. The major festival described by Wikipedia is the Pongala in the month of Vrischikam (November-December), when women cook rice, coconut and jaggery in earthen pots; the temple reports very large gatherings. Other observances include Thrikkarthika, Nirapara around Vishu, Panthrandu Noyambu from the first to the twelfth of Dhanu, and Naree Pooja. The temple is managed by a trust whose managing trustees include its chief priest, and a separate charitable trust, the Chakkulathamma Sanjeevani Ashramam Charitable Trust, runs social, education and health programmes.

description: The Nataraja Temple at Chidambaram, in Cuddalore district of Tamil Nadu, is a Shaiva temple where Shiva is worshipped as Nataraja, the lord of dance. The goddess Shivakama Sundari has her own shrine. According to Wikipedia, the temple is counted among the Pancha Bhuta Sthalams, with its sanctum linked to the element of space (akasha). The inner sanctum, the Chit Sabha, contains the Chidambara Rahasyam, a curtained space that devotees understand as representing the formless presence of the deity. The complex covers roughly 40 acres across four courtyards, with nine gopurams, halls such as the Kanaka Sabha and the thousand-pillared Raja Sabha, and the Sivaganga tank. According to Wikipedia, the temple drew patronage from Pallava, Chola, Pandya, Vijayanagara and Nayaka rulers over many centuries; the western gopuram is dated to about 1150 CE. The temple is praised in the Tevaram hymns. It is managed by the Podhu Dikshitars, its hereditary priests, whose management role has been the subject of administrative and legal disputes with the Tamil Nadu government, some of which are reported to be continuing. Margazhi Thiruvadhirai and Aani Thirumanjanam are among its major festivals.

description: Chottanikkara Temple stands at Chottanikkara, a suburb of Kochi in Ernakulam district, Kerala. The presiding deity is the Mother Goddess worshipped as Rajarajeswari, who according to Wikipedia is invoked as Saraswathi in the morning, Lakshmi at noon and Kali (Durga in Kerala Tourism's account) in the evening. The same pedestal also carries an image of Mahavishnu, which has given rise to the names Ammenarayana and Bhadrenarayana. Wikipedia states that the Cochin Devaswom Board administers the temple, and Kerala Tourism says it dates to the 10th century CE. Local legend tells of a forest tribesman, Kannappan, and his daughter Pavizham, and links the story to the origin of the shrine. Kerala Tourism highlights the Makam Thozhal festival, held on the Makam star in the Malayalam month of Kumbham (roughly mid-February to mid-March), and notes a popular belief that the Goddess relieves mental illness. Navarathri and Thrikarthika are also celebrated.

description: Kutralanathar Temple, also called Thirukkutralanathar, stands at Courtallam (Kutralam) in the Tenkasi area of Tamil Nadu, a town known for its waterfalls. It is a Shiva shrine where the deity is worshipped as Kutralanathar alongside the goddess Kuzhalvoimozhi Amman, according to the Tirunelveli district website. The temple is listed among the Thevaram-sung Paadal Petra Sthalams, and the same site records 89 inscriptions. Local tradition holds that the sage Agastya converted an earlier Vishnu image into a Shiva linga here, and the earliest Chola-period inscription calls the deity Thirukkutrala Perumal. Close by is the Chitra Sabha, a hall of Nataraja counted among the five Pancha Sabhas, with a copper-plated roof and paintings made with natural dyes. According to the same site, work on the hall began under Parakrama Pandiyan (1422-1483). The temple has five processional cars, and its listed festivals include the Chithrai Vishu, Aippasi Vishu and Thiruvathirai celebrations.

description: Sri Venkateswara Swamy Temple at Dwaraka Tirumala is a Vishnu temple dedicated to Venkateswara, set on the Seshachala hill in a village now listed under Eluru district, Andhra Pradesh (older references place it in West Godavari). The Sri Venkateswara Swamy Vari Devasthanam manages the temple. Tiru Kalyanotsavam is held twice a year, and Wikipedia also lists a Teppotsavam (float festival) in November.

description: Ekambareswarar Temple in Kanchipuram, Tamil Nadu, is a Shiva shrine where the deity is worshipped as a Prithvi (earth) lingam, with Parvati honoured as Elavarkuzhali. Devotional tradition holds that a mango tree in the precincts is about 3,500 years old, and local legend tells of Parvati's penance beneath a mango tree on the Vegavati's bank. The shrine is a Paadal Petra Sthalam, praised in the Tevaram hymns of Sambandar, Appar and Sundarar. Its main festival is Panguni Uthiram in March-April, culminating in the celebration of the divine wedding. The Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department of Tamil Nadu administers it; after major renovation, a consecration (Maha Kumbhabhishekam) was reported as held on 8 December 2025, the first in about 17 years.

description: The Ernakulam Shiva Temple, known to devotees as Ernakulathappan (Lord of Ernakulam), stands on the Durbar Hall Ground in central Kochi, Kerala. Wikipedia describes the presiding Shiva in the Gourisankara form, with a lingam regarded as self-manifested, and a sanctum that faces west toward the sea. Local tradition links the site to Arjuna's penance and to Shiva appearing as the hunter Kirata, and to a cursed sage who worshipped the buried lingam. The annual festival falls in the Malayalam month of Makaram, with flag hoisting, caparisoned elephants, panchavadyam and a ceremonial bath; Maha Shivaratri and Thiruvathira are also observed.

description: Gangaikonda Cholapuram, in Ariyalur district of Tamil Nadu, served as a capital under Rajendra Chola I, son of Rajaraja Chola I. Its Brihadisvara temple is dedicated to Shiva, worshipped as a lingam, with the goddess Periya Nayagi also honoured. According to Wikipedia, the temple was completed in 1035 CE, although some experts place construction earlier, near 1020. It follows the Dravidian style. Its nine-storey vimana rises about 55 metres, roughly three metres lower than the tower at Thanjavur, a difference that historians cited by Wikipedia read as deliberate, out of respect for his father's work. A large seated Nandi faces the sanctum. The sanctum walls carry reliefs, among which Nataraja and Saraswati are the most prominent, and the temple also preserves bronzes. It belongs to UNESCO's Great Living Chola Temples group, is maintained by the Archaeological Survey of India as a protected monument, and continues to host Saivite worship, with festivals such as Shivaratri, Aipassi Pournami and Thiruvadirai.

description: Basar, also spelt Basara, is a town in Nirmal district, Telangana, on the bank of the Godavari near the Maharashtra border. Its Gnana Saraswati temple is dedicated to Saraswati, goddess of learning, with an image of Lakshmi beside her in the sanctum and a Mahakali shrine nearby. According to Telangana Tourism, after the Kurukshetra war the sage Vyasa settled in the Dandaka forest, shaped sand images of Saraswati, Lakshmi and Kali, and the place is said to take its name from him. The present temple is reportedly the work of a Karnataka king, Bijialudu, and Wikipedia adds that idols were reinstated in the 17th century by a chieftain of Nandagiri after earlier destruction. The temple is widely used for aksharabhyasam, the ceremony in which children are introduced to writing before starting school. Daily worship begins around 4 am, and major festivals include Maha Shivaratri and Devi Navaratrulu. Wikipedia places the Basar railway station about 2.4 km away.

description: The Guruvayur Temple, in Guruvayur town, Thrissur district, Kerala, is dedicated to Guruvayurappan, a four-armed standing form of Vishnu worshipped as Krishna. According to Wikipedia, the roughly 1.2 m image is carved from shaligram stone and holds a conch, discus, mace and lotus. Tradition, drawing on the Gurupavanapura Mahatmya of the Narada Purana, holds that Vishnu created the idol, that Uddhava later retrieved it, and that Brihaspati and Vayu installed it at the present site. The temple is built in Kerala style, with a roof of copper sheets plated with gold. Its ritual system follows a framework formalised by Chennas Ravinarayanan Nambudiri (1427-1527), whose family holds the hereditary post of thantri. It was opened to all Hindus on 2 June 1947 following a temple-entry campaign led by K. Kelappan and A. K. Gopalan. The Guruvayur Devaswom, a statutory body, administers it under the Government of Kerala. Melpathur Narayana Bhattathiri's 16th-century Sanskrit work Narayaneeyam is associated with the temple.

description: Koodalmanikyam Temple is in Irinjalakuda, Thrissur district, Kerala. The presiding image is a four-armed form of Vishnu, generally believed to represent Bharata, brother of Rama, and worshipped as Sangameswara; the temple's own website explains the name Koodalmanikyam as the Malayalam rendering of that title. By tradition it belongs to the four-temple Nalambalam circuit, with Rama at Thriprayar, Lakshmana at Moozhikulam and Shatrughna at Payammal, which devotees visit together, especially in the month of Karkidakam. The earliest record is a stone inscription of the Chera king Sthanu Ravi, dated 854/55 CE, noting a land grant. The ten-acre walled complex has an eastern gopuram, a circular sanctum with a copper-plated roof and a Koothambalam, the temple theatre. According to Wikipedia, its customs differ from most Kerala temples, with three daily pujas and offerings limited to lotus, tulasi and thechi. The main annual festival is held in the month of Medam (April-May). Since 1971 a Government of Kerala-appointed committee, chaired by the Thrissur District Collector, has managed the temple through the Koodalmanikyam Devaswom.

description: The Jambukeswarar Temple at Thiruvanaikaval, in Tiruchirappalli district, Tamil Nadu, is dedicated to Shiva as Jambukeswarar and to Parvati as Akilandeswari. It is counted among the five Pancha Bhoota Sthalams, where the sanctum lingam represents water; the other four are at Kanchipuram, Chidambaram, Tiruvannamalai and Srikalahasti. Local tradition holds that Parvati fashioned a lingam of Kaveri water beneath a jambu tree and worshipped it here, and that two of Shiva's attendants, reborn as an elephant and a spider, were freed from a curse at the site; the name is explained as 'holy elephant forest'. The complex has five enclosures, and according to Wikipedia the fourth contains a hall of nearly 800 pillars. The sanctum is described as having a constant flow of water and is viewed through a stone window with nine openings. Inscriptions record Chola-era grants of the 11th and 12th centuries, with Hoysala work in the 13th. Sambandar, Appar and Sundarar sang here, and the temple is administered by the Tamil Nadu HR&CE Department.

description: The Kalugumalai Jain Beds are a group of rock-cut Jain reliefs on a rocky hill at Kalugumalai, a panchayat town in Thoothukudi district, Tamil Nadu. According to Wikipedia, the earliest work dates to the 8th century, in the reign of the Pandya king Parantaka Nedunjadaiya (768-800 CE), and the site belonged to the Digambara tradition. Around 150 niches and reliefs show Tirthankaras, including Parshvanatha flanked by two yakshas, and Gomateshwara. Labels and donor records are in the Vatteluttu script; Wikipedia counts 98 Jain inscriptions, 21 of them mentioning women mendicants, and the CPREEC heritage site notes donors ranging from artisans and cultivators to some high-ranking persons, as well as provision for teaching Jain doctrine. CPREEC says patronage declined after the 13th century. The Tamil Nadu Department of Archaeology maintains the beds as a protected monument. They are distinct from Vettuvan Koil, an unfinished 8th-9th century monolithic Shiva temple in the same town, and from the later Murugan temple, Kalugasalamoorthy.

description: Kanaka Durga Temple stands on Indrakeeladri hill beside the Krishna River in Vijayawada, NTR district, Andhra Pradesh. Its presiding deity is Kanaka Durga, shown with eight arms standing over the demon Mahishasura; according to Wikipedia, the main image is about 1.2 metres tall. Local tradition holds that the sage Indrakila did penance here and that the goddess made the hill her home. Both she and Malleswara Swamy, a form of Shiva, are described as self-manifested, and the goddess is placed to Shiva's right, which the Government of India's Utsav portal reads as a sign of Shakti's primacy. Wikipedia notes a Telugu inscription dated 1229 CE, of the Chola era, found at Veligandla village. The Dravidian-style complex also has shrines to Nataraja, Kartikeya and Hanuman. Dasara and Navaratri is the principal festival, with a boat festival; Varalakshmi Vratam and the Sakambhari festival are also observed. The Sri Durga Malleswara Swamy Varla Devasthanam manages the temple.

description: Kamakshi Amman Temple stands in the town of Kanchipuram, Kanchipuram district, Tamil Nadu, and is dedicated to Kamakshi, worshipped as a form of Parvati and as Shakti. Built in the Dravidian style on about five acres, it has a sanctum with a seated image of the goddess, with a Sri Chakra yantra in front that temple tradition credits to Adi Shankara. Smaller shrines honour Bangaru (Golden) Kamakshi, Adi Shankara and Saraswati, and a separate shrine is dedicated to Varaha. description: Kumari Amman Temple, also known as the Bhagavathy Amman Temple, stands in Kanyakumari town in Kanniyakumari district, Tamil Nadu, at the southern tip of mainland India where the Bay of Bengal, Arabian Sea and Indian Ocean meet. description: Keesaragutta Temple stands on a small hill at Keesara in Medchal-Malkajgiri district, Telangana, roughly 30 to 35 km from central Hyderabad, depending on the source. It is a Shiva temple whose main lingam is called Ramalingeswara; Telangana Tourism lists Bhavani and Sivadurga as his consorts, while Wikipedia names Parvati. According to local legend, Rama installed the lingam to atone for killing Ravana. Hanuman, sent to fetch a lingam from Varanasi, arrived late, so Shiva himself provided a self-manifested lingam. Hanuman is said to have scattered the lingams he brought, and many are still found on the hill and worshipped. Tradition also says Rama named the hill Kesarigiri after Hanuman's father Kesari, which became Keesara. Excavations near the temple have reported brick structures, lingas and fortification walls attributed to the Chalukya era, and Wikipedia mentions rock-cut caves and an early Telugu inscription dated on paleography to the 4th-5th century CE. Maha Shivaratri and the month of Karthika draw large crowds.

description: Sree Kurumba Bhagavathy Temple in Kodungallur, Thrissur district, Kerala, is dedicated to Bhadrakali, a fierce form of the Mother Goddess, locally called Kodungallur Amma. According to Wikipedia, the image faces north and has eight arms; the temple is regarded as head of 64 Bhadrakali kavus of Malabar. Traditions about its origin differ: one links the installation to Parasurama and the slaying of the demon Darika, while another identifies the goddess with Kannagi, whom the Chera king Senguttuvan is said to have enshrined in the Sangam period. Its best-known observances are the Bharani festival in the Malayalam months of Kumbham and Meenam, which features the Kavutheendal rite, and the four-day Thalappoli in Makaram. According to Wikipedia, ritual chicken sacrifice at the temple has been banned under Kerala law since 1978. The Cochin Devaswom Board took over administration in 1950, after earlier management by the Kodungallur royal family.

description: Kumbakonam, in Thanjavur district of Tamil Nadu, is often called a temple town, and Wikipedia counts about 188 Hindu temples within its municipal limits. The cluster includes Shaiva and Vaishnava shrines. Among the best known are the Adi Kumbeswarar temple, described by Wikipedia as the city's oldest Shaivite shrine, with origins traced to about the 7th century; the Nageswaraswamy temple, which has a separate Surya shrine; the Sarangapani temple, the largest Vaishnavite temple in the city with a twelve-tiered gopuram; and the Ramaswamy temple, noted for its Ramayana depictions and built under Govinda Dikshitar. Many of these temples are linked to the Mahamaham festival, held once every 12 years at the Mahamaham tank, which Wikipedia says drew over four million pilgrims in 2016. Two Shiva shrines on the outskirts, Kottaiyur Kodeeswarar and Sakkottai Amirthakadeswarar, are listed as Padal Petra Sthalams, sites praised in the Tevaram hymns.

description: Mahanandi is a village in Nandyal district, Andhra Pradesh, on the eastern side of the Nallamala hills. Its Mahanandiswara Swamy Temple is dedicated to Shiva and is one of the nine Nandi shrines of the area known as the Nava Nandulu, according to Wikipedia. The district administration dates the temple to the 7th century CE, and Wikipedia attributes the original structure to the Badami Chalukyas, with additions in later centuries and Vijayanagara-style elements. The temple is best known for its pushkarini ponds, which are fed by perennial springs; Wikipedia reports a steady water depth of about five feet, and the district page notes that objects on the pond floor remain visible. Nearby sites include the Kodandaramalayam and Kameswari Devi temples. The main annual festival, Maha Shivaratri, falls in February or March, and the temple draws pilgrims through the year.

description: The Poruvazhy Peruviruthy Malanada Temple is in Edakkad ward of Poruvazhy village, Kunnathoor taluk, Kollam district, Kerala. Its focus of worship is traditionally held to be Duryodhana of the Mahabharata. There is no idol and no sanctum; a raised platform, the althara, stands in the deity's place, and devotees worship through a personal act of resolve called sankalpam. Local tradition says Duryodhana, wandering in exile in search of the Pandavas, rested in these hills, was offered toddy by an elderly woman and then worshipped Shiva for the local people. Toddy is among the traditional offerings. The main festival, Malakkuda, falls in the Malayalam month of Meenam (March-April) and is known for the Kettukazhcha, in which large crafted figures are carried to the hill. According to Wikipedia, a ritual called Pallipaana is held once in twelve years, most recently in 2023. According to Wikipedia, the temple is run by the Malanada Devaswom, whose committee is elected by members of seven local karas.

description: The Meenakshi Sundareswarar Temple stands on the southern bank of the Vaigai River in Madurai, Tamil Nadu. Its presiding goddess is Meenakshi, regarded as a form of Parvati, who is worshipped alongside her consort Sundareswarar, a form of Shiva. According to Wikipedia, Tamil literature points to a shrine here by the mid-6th century CE, while the earliest surviving masonry dates to the Pandya ruler Sadayavarman Kulasekaran I, who reigned from 1190 to 1216. The complex was damaged during Malik Kafur's raid of 1311, was rebuilt under Vijayanagara rule, and was greatly expanded by the Madurai Nayaks in the 16th and 17th centuries. It covers about 14 acres of concentric walled enclosures with about 14 gopurams (towers), the tallest of them the southern tower at roughly 52 metres. It also has the Hall of a Thousand Pillars and the Golden Lotus Tank. The annual Chithirai festival includes the celebration of the divine wedding of Meenakshi and Sundareswarar. The temple is administered by the Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department of Tamil Nadu.

description: The Yogananda Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy Temple stands on the bank of the Krishna River at Mattapalli (Mattampally), in Suryapet district, Telangana, a district carved out of the former Nalgonda district. description: Nellaiappar Temple is a Shiva temple on the northern bank of the Thamirabarani River in Tirunelveli, Tamil Nadu. Shiva is worshipped as Nellaiappar and Parvati as Kanthimathi Amman, in separate shrines later linked by the Sangili Mandapam, which Wikipedia says was built in 1647. The original complex is traditionally credited to the Pandyas, with later contributions from the Nayaks and others. The temple is a Paadal Petra Sthalam praised in the Tevaram hymns of the Nayanmars, including Sambandar and Appar, and it is also listed as one of the Pancha Sabhai temples, associated with the copper hall (Thamira Sabhai). Major festivals include the Aani Brahmotsavam in June to July, the Aippasi Tirukalyanam and Arudra Darisanam. The HR&CE Department of Tamil Nadu administers the temple.

description: Sree Padmanabhaswamy Temple is a Vishnu temple in Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala. The deity is Vishnu as Anantha Padmanabha, shown reclining on the serpent Shesha, with Sridevi and Bhudevi. description: Arulmigu Dhandayuthapani Swamy Temple crowns Sivagiri hill in Palani, Dindigul district, Tamil Nadu, and is counted among the Six Abodes of Murugan. The presiding deity is Murugan as Dhandayuthapani, a youthful ascetic carrying a staff and wearing a loincloth. According to Wikipedia, the Sangam-era text Tirumurukarruppatai mentions the site as Thiruvavinankudi, and later dynasties including the Cheras, Cholas, Pandyas and Madurai Nayaks are associated with the temple; accounts of its earliest phase differ. Temple tradition holds that the sage Bogar fashioned the main idol from a compound of nine substances known as navapashanam. The sanctum is described as early Dravidian in style, and its vimana is gold-plated. Thaipusam, Panguni Uthiram, Vaikasi Visakam and Surasamharam are the major festivals, with kavadi carrying and tonsure prominent among devotional practices. The temple's prasadam, Panchamirtham, carries a Geographical Indication tag. Pilgrims can climb the steps or a sloping path, or use the winch or ropeway. The temple is administered by the Tamil Nadu government's Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department.

description: Parassinikadavu Muthappan Temple, also called Parassini Madappura, stands on the bank of the Valapattanam river in Parassinikadavu, Kannur district, Kerala, roughly 18 to 20 km from Kannur town, depending on the source. description: Pazhamudircholai Murugan Temple, also called Solaimalai Murugan Temple, is a hill temple on the outskirts of Madurai, Tamil Nadu, in the Alagar hills. It is dedicated to Murugan and is counted among the six Arupadaiveedu, the abodes of Murugan. According to Wikipedia, the temple originally honoured only the vel, Murugan's divine spear, and shrines to Murugan with his consorts Valli and Deivanai, and to Ganesha, were added later. A popular legend tells how Murugan, in disguise, shook a naaval tree to offer fruits to the poet Avvaiyar, who did not recognise him. The shrine is mentioned in early Tamil literature, including the Sangam-era Tirumurukarruppatai of Nakkeerar and the Silappatikaram, and in hymns of Arunagirinathar. Wikipedia states it is administered by the Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department of the Government of Tamil Nadu.

description: Phanigiri is an early historic Buddhist site on a hill at Phanigiri village, Nagaram mandal, Suryapet district, Telangana, about 40 km from Suryapet town. According to Wikipedia, it dates from the 1st century BCE to the 4th century CE and is related to the stupa complexes of Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda. The remains include a large stupa, apsidal chaitya halls with stupas, and monastic viharas. Reports describe sculpted panels of episodes from the Buddha's life and Jataka tales, Brahmi inscriptions, a life-size stucco Bodhisattva figure unearthed in 2019, and two large footprints believed to be the Buddha's. Excavations have yielded pottery, beads and coins of the Satavahana and Ikshvaku periods; in 2024 officials reported a pot of about 3,730 lead coins attributed to the Ikshvaku era. Deccan Chronicle describes the site as a centre of both Hinayana and Mahayana Buddhism. The same paper reported in June 2026 that the Telangana heritage department was to launch a conservation programme here, funded through corporate social responsibility money, after a foundation stone ceremony on 22 June.

description: The Pydithalli Ammavari Temple is in Vizianagaram town, Andhra Pradesh, near the Pedda Cheruvu tank. The goddess Pydithalli Ammavaru is regarded by local people as the village deity of Vizianagaram. According to local tradition, she was Pydimamba, a sister of the Vizianagaram ruler Vijaya Rama Raju, who died around the time of the Battle of Bobbili in 1757; accounts differ on the details, and Wikipedia notes there is no reliable evidence about her birth or personal life. One telling holds that fishermen later found her image on the western bank of the tank; the festival includes an umbrella made of fishing nets associated with the fishermen's community. The temple is best known for the Sirimanotsavam, held on the first Tuesday after Vijayadashami. A tall wooden pole, the sirimanu, is carried in procession between the temple and the fort with the temple priest seated atop it, while the Vizianagaram royal family watches from the fort. Wikipedia reports that the festival draws about two to three lakh visitors.

description: Rajarajeswaram, today better known as the Brihadisvara (Brihadeeswarar) Temple, stands in Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu, on the south bank of the Kaveri. It is a Shaiva temple built by the Chola emperor Rajaraja I. UNESCO records construction beginning around 1003-1004 CE and consecration around 1009-1010 CE. The name Rajarajesvaram means the temple of the lord of Rajaraja; locals also call it Peruvudaiyar Kovil or Thanjai Periya Kovil. Built of granite in Chola style, it has a 16-storey vimana, a monolithic Nandi weighing about 25 tonnes and a linga about 8.7 metres high; sources give slightly different heights for the tower, around 60 metres or more. Tamil and Grantha inscriptions record many gifts to the temple, and Chola-era frescoes inside the temple were rediscovered in 1931. UNESCO inscribed the temple as a World Heritage property in 1987, and the listing was extended in 2004 to form the Great Living Chola Temples with Gangaikondacholapuram and Darasuram. According to Wikipedia, the Archaeological Survey of India protects the monument, while the Thanjavur palace Devasthanam, through a hereditary trustee, manages the temple. Maha Shivaratri and the Brahan Natyanjali dance festival are observed here.

description: Ramanathaswamy Temple is on Rameswaram island in Ramanathapuram district, Tamil Nadu, and is reckoned among the twelve Jyotirlinga shrines of Shiva. Its presiding deity is Ramanathaswamy, with the goddess Parvathavardhini. According to tradition drawn from the Ramayana, Rama worshipped Shiva here; the sanctum holds a sand lingam attributed to Rama or Sita, depending on the telling, and a lingam said to have been brought by Hanuman. Wikipedia lists it among the Paadal Petra Sthalams sung by Appar, Sundarar and Sambandar, and among the Char Dham pilgrimage sites. The present structure grew over centuries, with contributions credited to the Pandyas, Sri Lankan and Jaffna rulers, and the Setupatis of Ramanathapuram, one of whom built the third corridor in the late 18th century. Wikipedia reports corridors totalling about 3,850 feet, an outer corridor with roughly 1,212 pillars, and 22 sacred theerthams inside the temple.

description: Sabarimala Sree Dharma Sastha Temple stands on a hill about 1,260 m high in Ranni taluk, Pathanamthitta district, Kerala, and is dedicated to Ayyappan, also known as Dharma Sastha. Wikipedia says it is managed by the Travancore Devaswom Board, an autonomous statutory body, while the Thazhamon Madom family holds traditional authority in religious matters. The main pilgrimage is the 41-day Mandala season, and the temple also opens for Makaravilakku on 14 January and for the first five days of each Malayalam month. Pilgrims climb eighteen sacred steps, which by custom are reserved for those carrying the irumudikkettu. Entry of women aged 10 to 50 was restricted by custom; the Kerala High Court upheld this in 1991. On 28 September 2018 the Supreme Court, by 4:1, held the restriction unconstitutional in Indian Young Lawyers Association v State of Kerala, with Justice Indu Malhotra dissenting. A review bench referred wider questions to a larger bench in November 2019. A nine-judge bench heard the reference in April and May 2026 and reserved judgment on 14 May 2026; at the time of writing no judgment had been reported.

description: Simhachalam Temple, formally the Sri Varaha Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy Temple, is a Vishnu temple on the Simhachalam hills near Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh. Its main deity is Varaha Narasimha, a combined form of Vishnu, with Lakshmi worshipped as Simhavalli Thayar. According to Wikipedia, the image is covered in sandalwood paste for most of the year and resembles a lingam. Local tradition, the Sthala Purana, credits Prahlada with the original shrine. The earliest inscription Wikipedia mentions dates to 1087 CE, and the Eastern Ganga king Narasingha Deva I is credited with rebuilding much of the present temple in the 13th century. The Visakhapatnam district website notes Chola, Velanadu and Eastern Ganga associations. Wikipedia describes an architectural mixture of Eastern Ganga, Eastern Chalukya and Chola styles, a west-facing temple and nearly 500 inscriptions. Chandanotsavam, held on Akshaya Tritiya, is a major festival at which the paste is removed. According to Wikipedia, the Simhachalam Devasthanam board administers the temple, with members of the Pusapati Gajapathi family as hereditary trustees.

description: This multi-level Shiva complex in Sirkazhi, Mayiladuthurai district, Tamil Nadu, is known variously as the Sattainathar or Brahmapureeswarar temple. According to Wikipedia it has three shrines on three levels: Brahmapureeswarar at the base, Thoniappar with the consort Periyanayaki in the middle, and Sattainathar, worshipped as Bhairava, above. Local tradition derives the name Thoniappar from a legend in which Shiva carried the 64 arts on a raft (thoni) at the time of the cosmic deluge. The temple is a Paadal Petra Sthalam: the child-saint Thirugnanasambandar is traditionally held to have been born in Sirkazhi, and the town has 71 Tevaram hymns, mostly his, according to the TN Temples Project. Wikipedia dates the entrance porch to the 10th-11th centuries, with Chola enlargements between the 11th and 13th. The Dravidian complex has seven-tiered gopurams and numerous water bodies, and eight Bhairava images are enshrined. Dharmapuram Adheenam, a Saivite mutt, is recorded as maintaining it. A ten-day festival takes place in the Tamil month of Chithirai.

description: Siruvapuri, near Chinnambedu in Thiruvallur district, Tamil Nadu, has a temple to Balasubrahmanya, a name of Murugan. According to the Dinamalar temple directory, the standing image is about 4.5 feet tall and is shown hand in hand with his consort Valli. Shrines to Shiva as Annamalaiyar and Parvati as Unnamulai Ambal stand to the right of the main sanctum, and a sanctum for the poet-saint Arunagirinathar faces it. Wikipedia reports that temple records date the structure to more than five centuries ago, and that Arunagirinathar, the 14th-century poet, is said to have visited several times and sung verses from his Thiruppugazh here. Local tradition links the place to the Ramayana: Dinamalar records a tradition that Lava and Kusa, the sons of Rama, were born here, whereas Wikipedia says only that they visited. According to Dinamalar, worship on Poosam star days is believed to help marriage prospects, as the wedding of Murugan and Valli is said to have fallen on a Poosam day, and devotees offer milk abhishekam in thanksgiving when their wishes are fulfilled.

description: Sittannavasal, in Pudukkottai district, Tamil Nadu, is a Jain site centred on the rock-cut Arivar Koil, a cave shrine of the Arihants associated with Tamil Shramana monks; Wikipedia explains the village name as 'abode of great saints', though scholars differ on its derivation. The west-facing cave has an ardha-mandapa and a small cubical sanctum whose reliefs show seated Tirthankaras beneath triple umbrellas and a teacher (acharya) in a niche, while a relief of Parshvanatha, the 23rd Tirthankara, appears under a five-hooded serpent. Scholars differ on its date: it has been attributed to the Pallava king Mahendravarman I (580-630 CE) or to a Pandya patron, with a 9th-century Pandya extension and an inscription of about 815 CE recording repairs by the acharya Ilam Gautaman. Fresco-secco paintings on the ceiling show a lotus tank with fish, birds and elephants, which some scholars read as the Samavasarana, the divine assembly hall of a Tirthankara. Nearby are the Ezhadipattam rock beds with Brahmi inscriptions, used by Jain ascetics for austerities. The Archaeological Survey of India maintains the site.

description: The Vadakkunnathan Temple stands on raised ground in the centre of Thrissur, Kerala, within a stone wall enclosing about nine acres. Shiva is the main deity, with Parvati, Shankaranarayana, Rama and Ganesha among the shrines in the complex. According to local tradition, the sage Parashurama founded the shrine, and no construction date is recorded in the sources consulted, so the temple's origin rests on tradition. The Thrissur district website and Wikipedia describe it as a classical example of Kerala architecture, with gopurams on four sides, a koothambalam theatre hall and Mahabharata murals. The lingam is traditionally covered by a large mound of ghee built up from daily abhishekam. According to Wikipedia, the temple and its murals are declared a National Monument under the AMASR Act, and a conservation project completed in 2015 received a UNESCO Asia-Pacific award. Thekkinkadu Maidan, the ground surrounding the temple, is the main venue of the Thrissur Pooram, and Maha Shivaratri is described as the temple's principal festival.

description: Srimulavasa (Sri Mulavasam, also Tirumulavata) was a Buddhist vihara and pilgrimage centre on the Kerala coast in the early medieval period. Scholars place it somewhere along the Alappuzha coast, between Ambalappuzha and Thrikkunnappuzha; its exact site is not fixed in these sources. It is known chiefly from the Paliyam copper plates, dated on the currently accepted view to 898 CE, in which the Ay king Vikramaditya Varaguna granted land to the vihara. The bilingual Tamil and Sanskrit plates open with verses honouring the Buddha, the Dharma-Sangha and Avalokitesvara. The Mushika Vamsa Kavya, composed around the 11th century, also mentions the shrine and says an Ezhimala prince protected it from the sea with stone blocks. A Buddha image found in Gandhara bears an inscription naming Mulavasa Lokanatha of the southern country, which Wikipedia reads as a sign of the centre's wider standing.

description: Srikalahasti Temple is a Shiva temple in Srikalahasti town, Tirupati district, Andhra Pradesh, about 36 km from Tirupati. Shiva is worshipped as Srikalahasteeswara and Parvati as Gnana Prasunambika. It is counted among the five Pancha Bhoota Sthalams, where the presiding linga is associated with air (Vayu), and is known as a Rahu-Ketu kshetra, where rituals to mitigate the influence of these two shadow planets are offered. Incredible India dates the inner temple to the 5th century, attributes the outer temple and main structure to Rajendra Chola I in the 11th century and credits the Vijayanagara Empire with the tall rajagopuram. According to Wikipedia, the Vijayanagara king Krishnadevaraya is credited with the main gopuram and a hundred-pillared hall, dated 1516 CE. The main gopuram, about 37 m (120 ft), collapsed on 26 May 2010 and was rebuilt and consecrated on 18 January 2017. The temple follows the Dravidian style. A 13-day Brahmotsavam coinciding with Maha Shivaratri is among its major festivals.

description: Sri Ranganathaswamy Temple stands on Srirangam island between the Kaveri and Kollidam rivers, near Tiruchirappalli in Tamil Nadu. It is dedicated to Ranganatha, a form of Vishnu, with his consort Ranganayaki, and UNESCO's tentative-list entry ranks it first among the 108 Divya Desams of the Vaishnava tradition. That entry describes a Dravidian complex of seven concentric enclosures over about 156 acres, with 21 gopurams, around 50 sub-shrines, several sacred pools and a Vijayanagara-period hall of pillars. The 13-tier Rajagopuram rises roughly 72-73 metres and, according to Wikipedia, was completed in 1987. More than 640 published inscriptions record patronage by Chola, Pandya, Hoysala and Vijayanagara rulers, among others. UNESCO's text places the temple's origin in the 1st century CE, while Wikipedia notes that the inscriptions range from about the 7th to the 17th centuries. Wikipedia also records a rebuilding in 1371 under the Vijayanagara commander Kumara Kampana. The Tamil Nadu HR&CE Department administers the temple. Its Margazhi Pagal Pathu and Ra Pathu festival, which includes Vaikunta Ekadashi, is a major observance.

description: The Bhramaramba Mallikarjuna Temple at Srisailam, in Nandyal district, Andhra Pradesh, is dedicated to Shiva as Mallikarjuna and to Parvati as Bhramaramba. description: Swaminatha Swamy Temple at Swamimalai, near Kumbakonam in Thanjavur district, Tamil Nadu, is dedicated to Murugan in his form as Swaminatha, a name linked to the tradition that he taught his father Shiva. It is counted among the Arupadaiveedu, the six abodes of Murugan. According to tradition, Murugan explained the meaning of the Pranava mantra, Om, to his father Shiva here, which gives the deity his name. The shrine crowns an artificial hillock about 18 metres high, reached by 60 steps that are said to correspond to the years of the Tamil sixty-year cycle. The main image, about 1.8 metres tall, holds a staff, and the vehicle shown is an elephant rather than the usual peacock. Shrines of Sundareswarar and Meenakshi stand at the foot of the hill. description: The Thillai Nataraja Temple stands in Chidambaram, Cuddalore district, Tamil Nadu, and is dedicated to Shiva as Nataraja, lord of the cosmic dance. According to Wikipedia, Shiva is worshipped here chiefly in anthropomorphic dancing form rather than as a linga (a small crystal linga is also kept in the Chit Sabha), and the temple is mentioned in hymns of the seventh century. The earliest verifiable inscriptions date to the early tenth century under the Chola king Aditya I, and the present complex took much of its form in the Chola period, with later work by Pandya, Vijayanagara and Nayaka patrons. It covers about 16 hectares within four concentric courtyards and has nine gopurams, the eastern one carrying 108 reliefs of classical dance postures. The Chit Sabha sanctum, the thousand-pillared hall and the Shivaganga tank are among its key features. The TN Temples Project lists a Govindaraja Perumal shrine, a Vaishnava Divya Desam, inside the complex. Wikipedia describes the Dikshitar community as its hereditary priests and trustees.

description: Thiruparankundram Subramaniya Swamy Temple lies at the foot of a rocky hill in Thiruparankundram, a suburb of Madurai, Tamil Nadu. description: The Subramaniya Swamy temple at Tiruttani (also spelled Thiruthani) stands in Thiruvallur district, Tamil Nadu, and is counted among the six abodes of Murugan (Arupadaiveedu). description: The Thousand Pillar Temple, also called Rudreshwara Swamy Temple or Veyyi Sthambhala Gudi, stands at the foot of Hanamkonda hill in Hanamkonda, Warangal region, Telangana. description: Paramekkavu Bhagavathy Temple is a Devi shrine in Round East, Thrissur, Kerala, and one of the two principal participants in the Thrissur Pooram. description: The Sree Rama temple at Triprayar, in Thrissur district, Kerala, stands on the bank of the Karuvannur river (also called the Thirupurayar), a few kilometres from the Arabian Sea. According to Wikipedia, it is one of the four temples of the Nalambalam Yatra, dedicated to Rama and his brothers Bharata, Lakshmana and Shatrughna. A traditional account recorded on a devotional blog says fishermen found the four images in the sea and gave them to Vakkayil Kaimal, a minister of the Ayiroor Kovilakam, who installed them at Triprayar, Moozhikulam, Irinjalakuda and Payammal. The presiding image is described there as a four-armed stone figure covered in panchaloha, holding a conch, discus, mace and rosary. Devotees feed fish in the river on the temple's east side, a rite called meenootu. The same blog names Triprayar Ekadasi, in the Malayalam month of Vrischikam, as the most important festival. The temple was once under the Zamorins, later passed to the Dutch, the Mysore rulers and the Cochin rulers, and is now governed by the Cochin Devaswom Board.

description: Vaitheeswaran Koil is a Shiva temple in the town of Vaitheeswarankoil, near Mayiladuthurai in Tamil Nadu. Shiva is worshipped as Vaidyanathar or Vaitheeswaran, interpreted as the God of healing, with his consort Thaiyalnayaki; Murugan as Muthukumaraswamy, Dhanvantari and Angaraka also have shrines. According to Wikipedia, it is one of the nine Navagraha temples of Tamil Nadu, associated with Mars (Angaraka), and local tradition holds that Angaraka was cured of leprosy here. The temple is praised in the seventh-century Tevaram hymns of Thirunavukkarasar and Sambandar and is classified as a Paadal Petra Sthalam. The Dravidian complex has a five-tiered gopuram, a sacred tank called Siddhamirtham and a neem as its sacred tree. Five inscriptions, mostly from the reign of Kulothunga Chola I (1070-1120 CE), record gifts and renovations. Wikipedia states that the Dharmapuram Adheenam, a Saiva monastic order, maintains the temple, and that Brahmotsavam is held in the Tamil months of Pankuni and Thai. The town is also known for palm-leaf (nadi) astrology, traditionally attributed to the sage Agathiyar.

description: The Janardanaswamy Temple at Varkala, in Thiruvananthapuram district, Kerala, is a Vishnu shrine where the deity, Janardanaswamy (also called Varkaleswara locally), is shown standing, facing east, with four arms; Sridevi and Bhudevi are in the main shrine. According to Wikipedia, tradition credits Brahma with founding the temple and a Pandya king with restoring it, while an inscription records partial renovation under Umayamma Rani (1677-84 CE); the claim of very great antiquity is unreferenced there. One legend explains the town's name from the bark garment (valkalam) that the sage Narada dropped here. The architecture is described as Pandya-Kerala in style, with a circular sanctum under a conical copper dome and a square mandapa carrying wooden Navagraha carvings. Devotees regard the place as suited to ancestral rites, so Varkala is called Dakshina Kashi and Dakshina Gaya, and bathing at nearby Papanasam beach is believed to wash away sins. The ten-day Arattu festival in Meenam opens with flag hoisting and ends with the deity's holy bath in the sea.

description: Sri Raja Rajeshwara Swamy Temple is in Vemulawada, in Rajanna Sircilla district of Telangana, about 38 km from Karimnagar. Devotees know the presiding deity, a form of Shiva, as Rajanna, with Raja Rajeshwari Devi and Ganesha also enshrined and Anantha Padmanabha Swamy as guardian deity, according to Telangana Tourism. Vemulawada was the capital of the Vemulawada Chalukyas, who Wikipedia says ruled from 750 to 973 CE; local legend credits a king named Raja Narendra with building the temple after a vision. The site is also called Dakshina Kasi and Harihara Kshetram because of its Shaiva and Vaishnava shrines. A well-known offering is Kode Mokku, in which devotees lead a bull around the temple, and pilgrims traditionally bathe in the Dharma Gundam tank before darshan. A dargah within the temple precincts is cited by Telangana Tourism as a symbol of religious tolerance. Maha Shivaratri is a major festival, along with Sri Rama Navami and Bathukamma.

description: The Kanaka Durga Temple stands on Indrakeeladri hill beside the Krishna river in Vijayawada, Andhra Pradesh. The goddess Kanaka Durga is shown in her eight-armed Mahishasura Mardini form. According to the national culture portal, she and Malleswara, a form of Shiva, are enshrined together as self-manifested deities, with Durga placed to Malleswara's right. According to Wikipedia, legend holds that the sage Indrakila performed penance and the goddess agreed to dwell on his hill to protect the region from demons. Wikipedia also notes a Telugu inscription dated 1229 CE, found at Veligandla, that records a donation to Malleswaradeva at Indrakiladri. The complex includes shrines to Nataraja, Kartikeya and Hanuman. The temple is administered by the Sri Durga Malleswara Swamy Varla Devasthanam. Dasara (Navaratri) is the main festival, with the goddess adorned in special alankaram forms on successive days and a boat festival (Teppotsavam) following the processions, while Sakambhari in Ashadha and Varalakshmi Vratam in Sravanam are also observed.

description: The Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy temple at Yadagirigutta, in Yadadri Bhuvanagiri district, Telangana, stands on a hillock roughly 60 km from Hyderabad and is dedicated to Narasimha, an avatar of Vishnu. According to the Skanda Purana as summarised by Wikipedia, the sage Yada did penance here and Narasimha appeared in five forms: Jvala, Gandabherunda, Yogananda, Ugra and Lakshmi Narasimha, which is why it is also called Pancha Narasimha Kshetram. The deities are enshrined in a cave sanctum. Sources describe its worship as following Vaishnava Agama traditions, variously given as Tenkalai or Pancharatra. A major reconstruction in black stone ran from 2016 and was completed in March 2022, after which the temple was inaugurated by the then Chief Minister; Wikipedia reports the cost as about 1,800 crore rupees and the expansion from roughly 2 to 16 acres. The Brahmotsavam is described by Incredible India as the main annual festival.

description: Sri Yaganti Uma Maheswara Temple is at Yaganti near Banaganapalle in Nandyal district, Andhra Pradesh, roughly 100 km from Kurnool, according to Wikipedia. Shiva and Parvati are worshipped together as Uma Maheswara in a single stone, with Nandi also venerated. Wikipedia attributes the temple to the 15th century and the Sangama rulers Harihara and Bukka Raya of Vijayanagara, but marks this as uncited. Local legend says the sage Agastya meant to install a Venkateswara image here but its toenail broke, after which Shiva declared the site suited to him because it resembled Kailash. A large stone Nandi stands before the temple, and devotees believe it is slowly growing; this is local belief rather than an established fact. A small pond, the Pushkarini, is fed by water flowing through a Nandi's mouth, and nearby caves are associated with Agastya, Venkateswara, Veerabrahmendra and Chitteppa. The Nandyal district website notes that Maha Shivaratri draws large crowds.
